books.section: Background to American Involvement in Vietnam
The Nature of the Vietnam War

primary_sources: Geneva Accords, Final Declaration of the Geneva Conference, July 21, 1954 (paraphrased)
Dwight D. Eisenhower, news conference, April 7, 1954 (paraphrased)
Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, Public Law 88-408, August 7, 1964 (paraphrased)

source: original; documents are paraphrases of public sources (see each document's sourcing note); the photograph is a public-domain U.S. Army photograph viewed before writing

stimulus.source_note: DBQ: documents below are the stimulus.

prompt: Evaluate the extent to which American involvement in Vietnam from 1954 to 1973 was driven by the policy of containment.

documents.title: Divided until the elections
documents.source: Paraphrase of the Final Declaration of the Geneva Conference, July 21, 1954.
documents.sourcing: The accords were written by the powers settling the French war, so they treat the division as a temporary regrouping, not a permanent border — the promised elections are the point the argument turns on.
documents.text: Paraphrase of the Final Declaration of the Geneva Conference, July 21, 1954. The accords ended the French war in Indochina and divided Vietnam at the 17th parallel into a Communist North and a non-Communist South. The division was temporary: general elections were to be held in July 1956, under international supervision, to reunify the country. The elections were never held.

documents.title: Falling dominoes
documents.source: Paraphrase of President Dwight D. Eisenhower's news conference, April 7, 1954.
documents.sourcing: Eisenhower is explaining to reporters why Indochina matters, so he stresses the spread of communism and the loss of raw materials, not Vietnamese nationalism.
documents.text: Paraphrase of President Dwight D. Eisenhower's news conference, April 7, 1954. Eisenhower said that if one country in Southeast Asia fell to communism, the countries around it would follow, like a row of dominoes. He argued that losing Indochina would cost the free world tin, tungsten, and rubber, and would put Japan's trade at risk.

documents.title: Power to make war
documents.source: Paraphrase of the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, Public Law 88-408, passed August 7, 1964.
documents.sourcing: Congress is handing the president broad war powers on the strength of his report, so the resolution shows containment turning into open war.
documents.text: Paraphrase of the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, passed August 7, 1964. After reports that North Vietnamese boats had fired on American destroyers, Congress gave President Lyndon Johnson power to take all necessary steps, including the use of armed force, to prevent further aggression in Southeast Asia. The House voted 416 to 0. The Senate voted 88 to 2.

documents.title: Patrol in the jungle
documents.source: Photograph: U.S. Army troops on patrol in the Vietnam War. U.S. Army photograph, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.
documents.sourcing: An Army photograph of soldiers on patrol, showing the war as the troops themselves fought it, in dense cover against a hidden enemy.
documents.text: The photograph shows three American soldiers resting during a patrol in Vietnam. They wear helmets and mud-covered uniforms and sit among dense green vegetation, with rifles and ammunition belts across their chests.

documents.title: Promises shot down
documents.source: Paraphrase of Martin Luther King Jr., "Beyond Vietnam," Riverside Church, New York, April 4, 1967.
documents.sourcing: King is speaking as a moral leader to a church audience, so he judges the war by what it cost the poor at home, not by Cold War strategy.
documents.text: Paraphrase of Martin Luther King Jr., "Beyond Vietnam," April 4, 1967. King said the war was draining money and attention from the poor at home. He said, "The promises of the Great Society have been shot down on the battlefield of Vietnam." His stand against the war broke his close ties with President Johnson.

documents.title: Peace with honor
documents.source: Paraphrase of President Richard Nixon's policy of Vietnamization, announced November 3, 1969.
documents.sourcing: Nixon is speaking to the nation to defend a policy of withdrawal without defeat, so he stresses honor and a gradual handover, not a change of aim.
documents.text: Paraphrase of President Richard Nixon's policy of Vietnamization, announced November 3, 1969. Nixon promised "peace with honor." Starting in 1969, his policy replaced American troops with South Vietnamese troops, while American bombing continued. At the same time, Nixon widened the war into Cambodia and Laos.

documents.title: The war ends for America
documents.source: Paraphrase of the Paris Peace Accords, signed January 27, 1973.
documents.sourcing: The accords are a negotiated settlement, so they show the limits of containment: the United States left without the victory it had sought.
documents.text: Paraphrase of the Paris Peace Accords, signed January 27, 1973. The accords ended direct American fighting in Vietnam, and American troops left. Fighting between North and South Vietnam continued, and in April 1975 North Vietnamese forces took Saigon. In 1976 Vietnam was reunited as one Communist country.

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which American involvement in Vietnam from 1954 to 1973 was driven by the policy of containment, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent of containment's role does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the Cold War rivalry with the Soviet Union, the Truman Doctrine, or the Korean War as an earlier containment war.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument, or background from a later century, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing specific and relevant content from at least three documents, such as the domino theory, the Tonkin Resolution, and Vietnamization.
rubric.notEarned: Quoting or naming documents without describing what they show does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support the argument, including the Geneva Accords and the Paris Peace Accords.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or listing documents without connecting them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific and relevant example outside the documents, such as the advisory buildup under Kennedy, the Tet Offensive, or the War Powers Resolution.
rubric.notEarned: Naming an outside example with no specific detail, or repeating a document's content, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining the relevance of a document's author, purpose, audience, or historical situation for at least two documents, such as Eisenhower warning reporters about falling dominoes or the Geneva Accords treating the division as temporary.
rubric.notEarned: Restating a document's sourcing note without explaining why it matters does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for demonstrating a complex understanding, such as qualifying the thesis by showing that containment drove the involvement and also that Vietnamese nationalism limited what containment could achieve, or weighing containment against other motives such as credibility and domestic politics.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: Containment drove American involvement in Vietnam to a great extent, from Eisenhower's domino theory through the Tonkin Resolution to Nixon's Vietnamization, but it was not the whole story, since Vietnamese nationalism and the search for credibility also shaped the war, and containment itself failed to achieve its aim.
Context: The United States came out of World War II committed to stopping the spread of communism, first in Greece and Turkey, then in Korea, and by the 1950s in Southeast Asia.
Evidence: Document 1 shows the Geneva Accords dividing Vietnam pending elections that were never held, which frames the war as a fight over reunification as well as containment. Document 2 shows Eisenhower's domino theory. Document 3 shows containment turning into war powers. Document 4 shows the guerrilla war American troops actually fought. Document 5 shows King arguing the war drained the Great Society. Document 6 shows Nixon handing the war to Saigon's army. Document 7 shows the United States leaving without victory.
Outside evidence: Kennedy raised the advisor count from about 700 to about 16,000, the Tet Offensive shook public trust in 1968, and the War Powers Resolution of 1973 limited the president.
Complexity: Containment explains why the United States entered and stayed, but the war's nature as a Vietnamese struggle for independence explains why containment could not win it, so the policy drove the involvement and also set its limit.
